objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe the seven elements of the learning process the PTS lists (learning theories, characteristics of learning, principles of learning, levels of learning, learning physical skills, memory and transfer of learning) at the depth the FOI knowledge test and an instructor checkride expect, and show how each one shapes a real ground or flight lesson, including instrument training.
why: A flight instructor applicant must receive and log ground training on the fundamentals of instructing, starting with the learning process [[60:340|14 CFR 61.185]], and pass a knowledge test on them [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183]]. Holders of a flight or ground instructor certificate and certain teachers are exempt from both [[60:340|14 CFR 61.185]] [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183]]. The AIH says that to take a pilot from memorized facts to judgment and problem solving, an instructor needs to know how people learn [[25:52|AIH 3-1]]. On a flight instructor practical test, the PTS tells the evaluator to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], so you must use these ideas, not just define them.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner passed the knowledge test last month with a high score. Today she flies holds well over the home VOR, but when ATC assigns a hold at an unfamiliar fix she freezes and stares at one instrument. key_terms.def: A body of principles that psychologists and educators use to explain how people acquire skills, knowledge and attitudes [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
Learning by observation: watching, imitating and then modeling others. Bandura's four stages are attention, retention, reproduction and motivation [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].
Theory focused on what goes on inside the mind. Learning is a change in the way the learner thinks, understands or feels, not just a change in behavior [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].
Bruner's idea of revisiting basic ideas again and again and building on them in more sophisticated ways as the learner develops [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].
A derivative of cognitive theory: learners actively build knowledge and skills from their experiences instead of taking them in passively [[25:56|AIH 3-5]].
A moment when a person is particularly responsive to being taught something; part of the law of readiness [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].
The principle that what is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression, so the instructor must teach it correctly the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].
The level where the learner associates what was taught with other blocks of learning. The AIH says it should be the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].
Knowledge shown in doing something. The learner usually cannot put it into words, and it is built by extensive practice [[25:74|AIH 3-23]].
The speed of performing a task improves as a power of the number of times it is practiced: fast gains early, slower gains later [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].
Relating incoming information to concepts or knowledge already in memory. This is when actual learning begins [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].
Near transfer carries learning to closely related settings; far transfer carries it to different settings and to new problems that share a common structure [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

chunks.title: The seven items, and what learning is

body.p: This lesson follows the seven items the PTS lists for the Learning Process Task [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS I.A]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.B teaches the same AIH chapter from the CFI ACS and goes deeper on scenario-based training, perception, errors, distractions and the risks of poor instruction. This lesson adds the FOI test vocabulary and instrument training examples.

The AIH opens the chapter with Beverly. On her first day she knows facts but cannot explain them, flies as if from a memorized list and loses her place when interrupted. Months later she applies knowledge to problems, flies smoothly, handles interruptions, catches her own small errors and recognizes the importance of regular study and practice [[25:52|AIH 3-1]]. The point: to take a pilot from memorized facts to judgment and problem solving, an instructor needs to know how people learn [[25:52|AIH 3-1]].
**What learning is.** The AIH gives several definitions that say much the same thing [[25:53|AIH 3-2]]:

bullets: A change in the behavior of the learner as a result of experience. The behavior can be physical and overt, or intellectual or attitudinal [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
The process by which experience brings about a relatively permanent change in behavior [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
A process that depends on experience and leads to long-term changes in behavior potential: the possible behavior in a situation, not the actual behavior [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
A relatively permanent change in cognition that comes from experience and directly influences behavior [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].

check.q: Your instrument learner can say the definition of a stabilized approach word for word. Has she learned it?
check.a: Not necessarily. Learning is a change in behavior that comes from experience [[25:53|AIH 3-2]], and you cannot assume learners can apply what they know because they can quote the correct answer verbatim [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]. Watch her fly one.

chunks.title: Learning theories I: conditioning, social learning and behaviorism

body.p: **Learning theory** is a body of principles that psychologists and educators use to explain how people acquire skills, knowledge and attitudes. The AIH names classical conditioning, operant conditioning and social learning as primary learning theories [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].

head: Theory
What it says
Where it shows up in flight training
rows: Classical conditioning
Learning from an association between a neutral environmental stimulus and a natural stimulus. Pavlov's dog learned to respond to a metronome that was started before feeding [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]
The AIH gives no flight example. Know the definition for the knowledge test
Operant conditioning

An association between a behavior and its consequences: positive behavior brings a positive consequence, negative behavior a negative one, and the learner predicts future consequences from that [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]
The law of effect works the same way: behaviors with satisfying outcomes tend to be repeated [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]
Social learning
Learning by observation: watching, imitating and then modeling the actions of others (Albert Bandura) [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]
Learners generally imitate the instructor, so demonstrate a skill exactly the way they should practice it, safety procedures included [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]

body.p: Bandura's social learning theory has four stages [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]:

bullets: **Attention:** the observer pays attention to others in order to learn [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].
**Retention:** the observer remembers the behavior so it can be repeated later [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].
**Reproduction:** the observer produces the behavior, which may need more skill than was observed [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].
**Motivation:** the observer has a reason to reproduce it [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].

body.p: **Behaviorism** explains behavior entirely through observable, measurable responses to stimuli, so behavior can be predicted from past rewards and punishments (the 'carrot and stick') [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. In modern education it stresses positive reinforcement by someone other than the learner, and in aviation training that someone is the instructor [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. Its popularity has waned because research shows learning is more complex than a response to a stimulus; today it is used more to break unwanted behaviors than to teach [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].

callout.text: Application: social learning never switches off in the airplane. In the right seat of an instrument trainer, your own briefing, checklist and callout habits are the model the learner attends to, retains and later reproduces [[25:54|AIH 3-3]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The AIH also warns that learners pick up attitudes about aviation, good or bad, as incidental learning [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

check.q: A learner starts touching each gauge in turn during the run-up, just as she watched you do, though you never taught it. Which theory explains it, and which of Bandura's stages has she just shown?
check.a: Social learning: learning by watching, imitating and modeling. She has gone through attention and retention and is now in reproduction [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].

chunks.title: Learning theories II: cognitive theory and its branches

body.p: Modern learning theories grew out of two concepts: behaviorism and cognitive theory [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. **Cognitive theory** focuses on what goes on inside the mind: knowing, perceiving, problem solving, decision making and awareness. Learning is not just a change in behavior; it is a change in the way a learner thinks, understands or feels [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

head: Name or branch
Key idea
Instrument training use
rows: Dewey: reflective thought
Learning improves to the degree it comes from reflection, which leads the learner from the unclear to the clear [[25:55|AIH 3-4]]
After a missed approach, let the learner reflect before you comment. The best scenarios end with the learner reflecting on the mental process used [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]
Piaget: assimilation and accommodation

Old ideas meet new situations (assimilation) and get changed to fit them (accommodation). Resolving that tension is intellectual growth, so people develop cognitive skills by actively interacting with the world [[25:55|AIH 3-4]]
This is a basic premise of scenario-based training [[25:55|AIH 3-4]]. Application: let a VFR pilot's old habits meet instrument problems in realistic scenarios, not only in lectures
Bruner: known to unknown, spiral curriculum
Teach from the known to the unknown and from the concrete to the abstract. The spiral curriculum revisits basic ideas repeatedly in more sophisticated ways [[25:55|AIH 3-4]]
Start hood work from the attitude flying the learner already knows: read correctly, the instruments give essentially the same information as outside references [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
Bloom: taxonomy of the cognitive domain
Six levels from simplest to most complex: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation [[25:56|AIH 3-5]]
See the two levels chunks
Information processing

The brain works like a computer: it encodes, keeps and retrieves information, and lets habitual things go unnoticed, like rudder in a turn [[25:56|AIH 3-5]]. It studies learning mainly through memory [[25:56|AIH 3-5]]

Cognitive strategies grew out of this theory [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]. The AIH's example is a learner's strategy for avoiding inadvertent IMC at night: check weather before departure, get updates every hour, divert at the first suspicion of weather ahead [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]
Constructivism

Learners actively build knowledge from experience by matching new information with what they already know, in a learner-centered setting [[25:56|AIH 3-5]] [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. An experienced teacher still guides them, and it suits some learners and situations, not all [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]
Constructivism supports teaching HOTS and training based on problems or scenarios [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]

body.p: **Higher order thinking skills (HOTS)** are the last three Bloom levels: analysis, synthesis and evaluation. In aviation HOTS is commonly called aeronautical decision-making (ADM), and the absence of HOTS is a common thread in accidents [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. Teach HOTS inside real subject matter, from simple to complex, in the initial pilot program and in every program after it, which includes the instrument rating [[25:57|AIH 3-6]].
Which theory is right? The AIH's answer is that no one learning theory is good for all situations and learners, and aviation instruction should use a combination [[25:93|AIH 3-42]].

callout.text: Application: experts' cognitive strategies can be taught. Researchers found them by having experts think aloud while solving problems [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]. Brief an approach out loud the way an expert thinks it through, then have the learner do the same on the next one.

check.q: Which theorist would tell you to start a VFR pilot's instrument training from the attitude flying she already knows?
check.a: Jerome Bruner: teach from the known to the unknown, because people learn best by relating new knowledge to existing knowledge [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

body.p: Psychologists generally agree on many characteristics of learning. If learning is a change in behavior from experience, instruction has to be a careful, systematic creation of experiences that promote learning, and a learner's background strongly shapes how that person learns [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]. To be effective, a learning situation should be purposeful, based on experience, multifaceted and an active process [[25:70|AIH 3-19]].

**Learning is purposeful.** Each learner sees a lesson from a different viewpoint, shaped by past experience and goals. Learners learn from any activity that furthers their goals, and their needs and attitudes may decide what they learn as much as your lesson plan does, so relate new learning to their goals [[25:70|AIH 3-19]].

**Learning is a result of experience.** You cannot learn for the learner: knowledge cannot exist apart from a person, and two people watching the same event learn different things [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]. An experience that involves feelings, thoughts, memory of past experiences and physical activity teaches more than one where all the learner does is memorize [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]. A physical skill is learned only by actually doing it, and judgment only through experiences that require judgment on realistic problems [[25:70|AIH 3-19]].

**Learning is multifaceted.** Verbal, conceptual, perceptual, emotional and problem-solving elements can all happen at once [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]. Learners also pick up things you did not plan, such as attitudes about aviation, good or bad, or self-reliance. This incidental learning can have a great impact [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

**Learning is an active process.** Learners do not soak up knowledge like a sponge. Being in the classroom or airplane when you presented something does not mean they remember it, and quoting the correct answer verbatim does not mean they can apply it. They need to react and respond, outwardly or inwardly [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

callout.text: Application: one holding ground lesson can serve all four. Tie it to the learner's own trips (purposeful), give a real clearance and chart to work (experience), model a calm and careful briefing (multifaceted), and make the learner choose and explain the entry (active).

check.q: Your learner sat through your whole partial-panel briefing and nodded. Why does the AIH say that is not enough?
check.a: Learning is an active process. You cannot assume learners remember material just because they were present, or can apply it because they can quote it; they must react and respond [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

body.p: Right after the characteristics, the AIH covers learning styles. A learning style is a person's preference for understanding experiences and turning them into knowledge, and everyone has a mixture of strengths and preferences, not one style to the exclusion of others [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

bullets: **Approaches to Learning:** the approach depends on the learner's intentions, such as short-term memorization for a quiz or the long-term ability to use the material [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

**Right brain and left brain:** right-brain dominant people are described as spatially oriented, creative, intuitive and emotional; left-brain dominant as verbal, analytical and objective. It is a preference, not an absolute, and when learning is new, hard or stressful the brain tends to fall back on the preferred side [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

**Holistic and serialistic:** serialistic (left-brain) learners build understanding in linear, logical steps, a bottom-up strategy; holistic (right-brain) learners want the big picture first, a top-down strategy, learn in large jumps and are helped by analogies [[25:72|AIH 3-21]].
**Index of Learning Styles (Felder and Silverman):** sensing or intuitive, visual or verbal, active or reflective, sequential or global [[25:72|AIH 3-21]].
**VAK:** visual, auditory and kinesthetic, based on the three main sensory receptors. VARK adds reading and VAKT adds tactile [[25:73|AIH 3-22]].
**Superlinks (Linksman):** the VAKT styles combined with brain hemisphere preference into eight superlinks [[25:74|AIH 3-23]].

body.p: Learners generally use all three VAK styles, with one dominant, and the dominant style may change with the task [[25:73|AIH 3-22]]. Beverly's first landing used all three: visual cues to line up, listening as Bill talked her through, and the feel of the landing itself [[25:74|AIH 3-23]]. The AIH notes controversy over the scientific value of learning styles [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]. Its practical rule: make sure a variety of learning styles are addressed in every lesson [[25:74|AIH 3-23]].

callout.text: Application: an ILS lesson for every channel. Use the chart and a whiteboard sketch (visual), a talk-through where the learner verbalizes questions (auditory), and a demonstration followed by the learner flying it hands-on in a training device (kinesthetic). These follow the teaching tips in AIH Figure 3-16: graphs and charts, verbalized questions and demonstrations of skills [[25:73|AIH 3-22]].

check.q: A learner says she is a 'visual learner' and asks you to skip the spoken talk-through. What do you tell her?
check.a: Learners generally use all three styles, and the dominant one can change with the task [[25:73|AIH 3-22]]. You will address a variety of styles in every lesson, talk-through included [[25:74|AIH 3-23]].

chunks.title: Principles of learning: Thorndike's laws and three more

body.p: E. L. Thorndike set down three laws of learning in the early 20th century: readiness, exercise and effect. The AIH calls them universally accepted and applicable to all kinds of learning. Three more were added later: primacy, intensity and recency [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.A covers the human needs that sit under readiness.

head: Principle
What the AIH says
In instrument training
rows: Readiness

Basic needs must be met, and the learner must want to learn and have the needed knowledge and skill [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. Learners learn best when they see a clear reason [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Keep readiness up with clear objectives tied to each topic and a logical order that leaves a need for the next topic [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]

Learners often ignore trim until other tasks pull their attention away [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Trimming for hands-off flight is essential for smooth, precise aircraft control [[23:135|IFH 6-2]], so hood work makes the need obvious. Teachable moments can be found even in an instrument proficiency check [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]
Effect

Behaviors with satisfying outcomes tend to be repeated; undesired outcomes make them less likely [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Create situations that promote success, and praise progress before discussing what needs improving [[25:63|AIH 3-12]] [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]

The AIH's example of a weakened connection is teaching landings on the first flight [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Application: likewise, do not open an instrument course with a partial-panel approach in turbulence
Exercise
Connections strengthen with practice and weaken with disuse: use it or lose it. Practice is most meaningful inside a real-world application [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Pilots who are instrument rated but not instrument proficient are also susceptible to loss of control in IMC [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.5]]
Primacy

What is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression, so teach it correctly the first time. The first experience should be positive, functional and lay the correct foundation [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
In initial instrument training, emphasis on a single instrument is very common and can become a habit if not corrected [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Intensity

Immediate, exciting or dramatic learning tied to a real situation teaches more than a routine or boring experience. Realistic scenarios build proficiency in maneuvers, tasks and SRM [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Application: a realistic, rising-workload IFR arrival in a training device leaves a deeper mark than another lap of the same hold
Recency

Things most recently learned are best remembered. Plan a summary that repeats key points at the end of a lesson or postflight critique; in SBT, train as close as possible in time, and as much alike as possible, to the real scenario [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Application: end each approach lesson by restating the two or three points that matter most, and fly practice approaches shortly before a real IFR trip

callout.text: The AIH also lists five principles of retention: praise, association, favorable attitudes, learning with all senses and meaningful repetition [[25:89|AIH 3-38]] [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]. They are not the principles of learning. Keep the two lists apart in an oral exam.

check.q: On your learner's first hood lesson you insist that she briefs the approach fully and correctly. Which principle are you serving?
check.a: Primacy: what is learned first creates a strong, almost unshakable impression, so teach it right the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

chunks.title: Levels of learning: from rote to correlation

body.p: Every level starts with perception. All learning comes from perceptions through the senses, and it happens fastest when more than one sense is involved [[25:58|AIH 3-7]]. Perception is affected by the physical organism, goals and values, self-concept, time and opportunity, and the element of threat [[25:58|AIH 3-7]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.B covers each factor.

**Insight** is the grouping of perceptions into meaningful wholes, such as seeing that rpm, power setting, airspeed and pitch attitude in a fixed-pitch airplane all affect each other [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]. Instruction speeds insight by pointing out relationships as they occur, in a secure, nonthreatening setting [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]. Insight is the step out of rote: with instruction on the controls and experience in straight-and-level flight, Beverly consolidates old and new perceptions into an insight on turning, and then has understanding [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].
The AIH's four practical levels of learning [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]:

head: Level
What the learner can do
Key verbs
Instrument example (Application)
rows: Rote
Repeat what was taught without understanding or applying it. The fact level is a single concept [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Define, identify, label [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Recites the steps for setting up an approach
Understanding
Put two or more concepts together [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Describe, estimate, explain [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Explains why each setup step is there
Application
Put two or more concepts together to form something new [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]; for a skill, practice to consistency after a demonstration [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Determine, develop, solve [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Flies approaches to standard in the practice area
Correlation
Associate an element with other blocks of learning, earlier or future. This should be the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
The AIH lists none
Fits the approach into a real IFR flight with an amended clearance and a missed approach

body.p: Beverly's level turn shows the climb. Repeating Bill's five steps is rote; with instruction and experience she understands; after demonstration and practice to consistency she can apply it; using turn entries in the traffic pattern is correlation [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Application is a major level, and one where instructors too often stop. Moving on to other elements at that point is piecemeal instruction, which is usually inefficient [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

Rote still has a place: memorizing facts lets a learner get started quickly, but it fails on questions the facts do not cover [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]. Test-prep materials stress rote learning, the lowest of all levels, which is why some applicants pass the knowledge test easily yet show weak knowledge in the oral [[25:131|AIH 5-28]].

callout.text: Application: write each instrument lesson objective at a level, using the AIH verbs, because objectives should include the desired level of learning [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. 'Explain the holding entries' and 'fly the hold in an amended clearance' are different lessons.

check.q: Your learner flies holds well over the home VOR but cannot fit one into a real trip with a clearance change. What level has she reached, and what is the goal?
check.a: Application. The goal is correlation, tying the hold to other blocks of learning in a real flight [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Stopping here would be piecemeal instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

chunks.title: Bloom's levels and the three domains

body.p: Bloom grouped learning into three domains: cognitive (thinking), affective (feeling) and psychomotor (doing) [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. Each domain has its own levels.

**Cognitive.** Six levels from recalling facts to evaluation [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. The top three are the HOTS: analysis breaks information into parts (differentiate, compare, prioritize), synthesis puts parts together into a new whole (create, design, plan), and evaluation makes judgments about merit [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Ground school, reading, briefings and computer-based training usually reach the first three levels; analysis, synthesis and evaluation can be reached through SBT [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

**Affective.** The learner's emotions toward learning: feelings, values, enthusiasm, motivation and attitudes, including attitude toward safety and risk [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. Five levels: awareness, response, value, organizing and integration, ending when the learner internalizes what was taught [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. It is harder to measure, but motivation and enthusiasm matter in all learning [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

**Psychomotor.** Physical skill, built by repetitive practice and measured by speed, precision, distance and technique [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]. Flying a precision instrument approach and programming a GPS receiver are psychomotor skills, and as tasks grow more complex the need to integrate cognitive and physical skills grows [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]. Its levels are in the next chunk.

These levels can be tied to the ACS to show the level of knowledge or skill a task requires, and the AIH's list of action verbs for the three domains gives examples of performance-based objectives [[25:69|AIH 3-18]].

callout.text: Application: one instrument objective at each top level. Analysis: compare the weather at two possible alternates. Synthesis: design a personal minimums checklist for IFR departures. Evaluation: judge whether today's approach should be flown at all.

check.q: Your learner flies a good RNAV approach but treats the stabilized approach criteria as optional. Which domain needs work?
check.a: The affective domain: attitudes and values, including attitude toward safety and risk [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. The aim is for the learner to value the criteria and finally internalize them [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

chunks.title: Learning physical skills: levels and stages

body.p: The 9B covers the PTS item 'learning physical skills' [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS I.A]] in the psychomotor domain [[25:68|AIH 3-17]] and in Acquiring Skill Knowledge [[25:74|AIH 3-23]]. A physical skill can only be learned by actually performing it: pilots in training learn to fly only if their experiences include flying [[25:70|AIH 3-19]].

**Skill knowledge** shows up in doing. Unlike declarative knowledge, the learner is usually not aware of it and cannot put it into words; you see it only in performance, it rests on extensive practice, and it is acquired slowly [[25:74|AIH 3-23]].
Figure 3-12 shows a seven-level psychomotor taxonomy, but the AIH's practical levels for aviation training are four [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]:

bullets: **Observation:** the learner watches a more experienced person, noting sequences and relationships. Reading, video or computer-based training can add to it [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].
**Imitation:** the learner copies the skill under the instructor's watchful eye [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].
**Practice:** the learner repeats the activity over and over, possibly without direct oversight, like solo touch-and-goes [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].
**Habit:** reached when the learner can perform the skill in twice the time the instructor or an expert takes. Ability is evaluated with a performance or skill test [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].

body.p: **Stages of skill acquisition.** The AIH names three: cognitive, associative and automatic response, and you need to recognize each one to judge progress [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

head: Stage
What you see
On instruments
rows: Cognitive
Memorized steps, little sense of progress, fixation on one part. The skill takes all the learner's attention, and distractions make it deteriorate or stop [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
A beginner may cross-check rapidly without knowing what to look for [[23:144|IFH 6-11]], and beginning instrument pilots characteristically fixate on particular instruments [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Associative
Links steps to outcomes, checks progress and adjusts. Still deliberate, but handles distractions better [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Beverly's steep turn: still fighting the bank, she glances at the altimeter, sees almost 100 feet lost, adds back pressure and trims [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Automatic response
Rapid and smooth, with fewer and smaller adjustments. The learner can talk while doing it but may not be able to explain the steps [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
With proficiency, a pilot cross-checks mainly from habit, suiting scan rate and sequence to the situation [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]

body.p: The IFH applies the same idea to the two fundamental instrument skills, cross-check and interpretation: they are learned separately and in deliberate sequence, and a measure of proficiency is the ability to integrate them into smooth, positive control [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

check.q: Under the hood your learner holds altitude well until you ask for a frequency change, then the heading wanders 20 degrees. Which stage is she probably in, and what does that tell you?
check.a: The cognitive stage: the skill takes all her attention, so distractions make it deteriorate [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Fixation is often a sign the task needs more practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

chunks.title: Teaching a physical skill: telling and doing

body.p: In flight, the AIH applies the demonstration-performance method through the telling-and-doing technique. Its key addition is the step where the learner tells and the instructor does [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

bullets: **Instructor tells, instructor does.** A planned demonstration with explanation, flown in the same order you explained it. Learners imitate you, so demonstrate exactly the way they should practice, safety procedures included, and acknowledge at once any deviation from your explanation [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

**Learner tells, instructor does.** Free of flying the airplane, the learner organizes the steps, perceptions begin to become insights, and you see whether the learner understands. By the principle of primacy, fix a misunderstanding here, before the learner is busy controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

**Learner tells, learner does.** Learning happens and habits form here. The learner thinks aloud, which keeps you aware of the thinking and shows whether an error comes from a misconception or a simple lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: How to sequence it: most physical skills are explained in the same step-by-step order used to perform them. Use known to unknown when the skill builds on earlier ones, and simple to complex when teaching several skills at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Avoid jargon the learner does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

**Knowledge of results.** Learners need to know when they are right as much as when they are wrong, as soon after the performance as possible, and should not practice mistakes, because unlearning a mistake is harder than learning it right the first time [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. A long, detailed explanation before the learner tries is confusing; specific comments mean more once the skill is partly mastered [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

callout.text: Application: for a level-off from a climb under the hood, have the learner call each instrument and what it shows while you fly, then while she flies. If her calls are right but the level-off is late, it is motor skill; if the calls are wrong, it is a misconception [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Why put the 'learner tells, instructor does' step between your demonstration and her practice?
check.a: She can organize her thoughts without having to fly, perceptions start to become insights, and you can check her understanding and correct it before she is busy controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: Theories of skill learning agree that progress depends on repeated practice. The power law of practice says the speed of performance improves as a power of the number of trials: fast gains early, slower gains later [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. When the curve levels off for a while, that is a learning plateau [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

**Plateaus.** A plateau may mean capability limits, consolidation, lost interest or a need for a better method, and it does not necessarily mean learning has stopped. In motor skills it is normal [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Tell the learner ahead of time that it is normal and temporary, move to a different place in the syllabus for a while, explain the lesson and its reason better, and remember that over-practice can cause it [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

head: Type of practice
What it is
Instrument example (Application)
rows: Deliberate
Aimed at a goal, on specific areas, with specific feedback on the gap between actual and goal performance. Avoid distractions and keep feedback brief and explicit [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]
Several entries into the same hold, with a quick, specific note after each
Blocked
The same drill until it is automatic. Better short-term performance but poorer long-term learning, and it fools both learner and instructor [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
Six ILS approaches in a row that look better each time
Random
Different skills mixed through the session. It scores worse during practice but better on a test the next day, and well-written SBT encourages it [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
A hold, a nonprecision approach and a missed approach mixed in one IFR scenario

body.p: **How much practice.** A beginner reaches a point where more practice is unproductive or even harmful: errors increase and motivation declines. Experienced learners profit from longer periods [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Whether to break a practice period into parts depends on the nature of the skill [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Practicing the same skill in different settings adds new perceptions and insights [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

**Evaluation versus critique.** Early on, practical suggestions help a learner more than a grade, and early evaluation mostly checks your own teaching and finds strengths and weaknesses [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.B covers this in depth.

**Overlearning** is practice past the required level of excellence. It can streamline work, but a checklist recitation can come apart from the thoughts and actions it should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. A related FAA warning: automation can erode a complacent pilot's manual flight skills, so pilots of automated aircraft should fly by hand at times [[15:13|AC 61-98E 2.2.2]].

**Application of skill.** The final question is whether the learner can use it: the skill must be understood so well that it becomes easy, even habitual, and the learner must recognize when to use it, which is transfer of learning [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. To help learners acquire skills, the AIH says to explain that continued practice is the key, monitor practice and give immediate feedback, avoid conversation and distractions during individual skill practice, and explain that plateaus are common [[25:80|AIH 3-29]].

check.q: Six ILS approaches in a row looked better each time, but a week later they are rough. What happened, and what do you change?
check.a: Blocked practice: better short-term performance, poorer long-term learning [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Mix skills with random practice, such as a full IFR scenario [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

body.p: Memory is the ability to encode (first perception and registration), store (keep over time) and retrieve (use stored information) [[25:86|AIH 3-35]]. A widely accepted model has three parts: sensory memory, short-term memory (STM) and long-term memory (LTM) [[25:86|AIH 3-35]].

**Sensory memory** takes in stimuli and, within seconds, discards what seems extraneous and passes on what the person judges relevant. That preset filter is precoding: a fire alarm gets instant attention no matter what else is going on [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Dramatic input that hits more than one sense is more likely to make an impression [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].

**Short-term memory** holds information roughly 30 seconds and about seven chunks, like a seven-digit phone number. Coding takes 5 to 10 seconds, and if it is interrupted the information is easily lost [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Rehearsal (rote repetition) holds information; coding, or chunking, sorts it; recoding relates it to what is already known, and that is when actual learning begins [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. The AIH compares STM to the control tower of a major airport. Its three operations are iconic memory (brief visual images), acoustic memory (sounds, held longer than iconic) and working memory, the 'scratch-pad' that holds and manipulates information for immediate use [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].

**Long-term memory** is relatively permanent storage of unlimited information. Information gets there when it carries significance (the first solo), through repetition, or by being attached to something significant [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Good encoding gives meaning and links old and new, and LTM is a reconstruction, not a pure recall [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. It also holds psychomotor skills, which frees a pilot for navigation, ATC communication and scanning [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. LTM is organized in schemas, so activate them before new material, for example with a brief review of the previous lesson [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].

callout.text: Application: an IFR clearance is a short-term memory problem. An experienced pilot has a schema that expects five key items [[25:62|AIH 3-11]], and learners who know the format can build their own abbreviations to copy it [[25:102|AIH 4-9]]. Teach the format first, and stay quiet while the learner is coding it [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].

check.q: What happens if you start a conversation while your learner is still coding a clearance in short-term memory?
check.a: Coding takes 5 to 10 seconds, and if it is interrupted the information is easily lost, since STM keeps it only about 30 seconds [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].

body.p: **How usage affects memory.** Recall depends mainly on how often knowledge has been used (frequency) and how recently (recency) [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]:

bullets: **Frequency and recency:** used a lot before and still used. Retrieved easily and quickly [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].
**Frequency only:** used a lot before, not lately. Retrieved slowly or not at all until some recent practice refreshes it [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].
**Recency only:** newly learned. Very vulnerable, like throw-away information, until regular rehearsal builds frequency [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].

body.p: **Forgetting** is usually a failure to retrieve: the information is still somewhere in LTM [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. The theories [[25:88|AIH 3-37]] [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]:

head: Theory
What it says
rows: Retrieval failure
Knowing something but not being able to bring it up (tip of the tongue), plus information never encoded well enough to reach LTM (failure to store) [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]
Fading (decay)
Information not used for a long time fades away [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]
Interference
A newer experience or similar learning overshadows the old. Similar material interferes more than dissimilar, and material not well learned suffers most [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]
Repression or suppression
A memory is pushed out of reach to avoid its feelings. Repression is unconscious, suppression conscious [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]

body.p: **Retention of learning.** Teach thoroughly and with meaning; rote learning is superficial and not easily kept [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. The five retention principles: praise stimulates remembering, recall is promoted by association, favorable attitudes aid retention, learning with all senses is most effective, and meaningful repetition aids recall; some research indicates three or four repetitions give the maximum effect [[25:89|AIH 3-38]] [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

More memory facts the FOI test likes: retention drops after the first 10 to 15 minutes of a lesson until the last 5 to 10 [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]; mnemonics include acronyms, acrostics such as ANDS for a compass error, rhymes and chaining [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]; the more deeply learners think about material, the better they recall it (depth of processing) [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]; and shorter, regularly spaced study beats cramming, while even writing study questions helps [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].

**After training.** A certificate guarantees nothing: continued practice is the only way to keep knowledge and skill, and even skills that became automatic may not stay automatic after disuse [[25:92|AIH 3-41]]. In one study, pilots' memory of regulations was related to the months since their last flight review [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].

callout.text: Application: holds learned just before a six-week break had recency only, the kind most vulnerable to forgetting. Plan regular rehearsal over the next lessons to build frequency [[25:88|AIH 3-37]], and open each lesson with a short review to activate the schema [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].

check.q: A learner flew a new GPS unit last week and now mixes its menus with the old one he flew for years. Which theory of forgetting fits?
check.a: Interference: the learning of similar things has intervened, and similar material interferes with memory more than dissimilar material [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].

chunks.title: Transfer of learning and habit formation

body.p: **Transfer of learning** is the ability to apply knowledge or procedures learned in one context to new contexts. Bringing in earlier knowledge speeds learning and deepens understanding, and practicing under a variety of conditions gives positive transfer [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

bullets: **Near transfer:** from the setting where it was learned to closely related ones [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].
**Far transfer:** to a different setting, and to new problems that share a common structure with what was learned [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].
**Generativity:** the learner comes up with new solutions alone [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].
**Positive transfer:** learning skill A helps skill B, like slow flight helping short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
**Negative transfer:** learning skill A hinders skill B, like airplane approaches hindering helicopter approaches. Learning B can also affect A [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

body.p: Some transfer is involved in all learning, because new learning builds on previous experience, so you need to know each learner's past experience and current knowledge [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Plan for transfer by putting material in a meaningful sequence where each phase prepares for the next [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. The AIH's suggestions [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]:

bullets: Plan for transfer as a primary objective [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
Make sure learners understand the information applies to other situations, and prepare them to look for other uses [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
Keep high-order learning standards; overlearning may be appropriate [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
Avoid unnecessary rote learning, since it does not foster transfer [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
Give meaningful experiences that build confidence in transferring knowledge [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
Use material that forms valid concepts and generalizations and makes relationships clear [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

body.p: **Habit formation.** Correct habits from the start are essential, because primacy is one of the fundamental principles of learning, and proper habits are much easier to build than faulty ones are to correct later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Aviation training follows a building block concept: new learning rests on a solid foundation of old learning [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

**Instrument examples.** Integrated flight instruction, which teaches each maneuver by outside and instrument references from the first lesson, builds habits that give a firm foundation for later instrument rating training [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. You must also make sure learners understand that this introduction does not prepare them for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Understanding transfers too: once the role of each instrument is learned, a pilot is better equipped to handle failure of key instruments [[23:135|IFH 6-2]], and learners who understand a process master variations such as new avionics more easily [[25:61|AIH 3-10]]. Since formats are not standardized, moving from one manufacturer's avionics to another should give a pilot pause [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

callout.text: Application: when a learner trained on round gauges moves to a glass panel, ask what she already knows and plan blocks that build on it [[25:147|AIH 7-3]], then practice the differences under varied conditions [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

check.q: Your learner trained VFR with integrated instruction from the first lesson. How does that help him now, and what should he have been told back then?
check.a: The habits of cross-check, interpretation and control give a firm foundation for the instrument rating [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. He should also have been told that this introduction did not prepare him for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Social Learning: simply, learning by observation; learning by watching, imitating, and modeling the actions of others and associating consequences to those observed behaviors.

II Comprehension, explaining the meaning of information: describe, generalize, paraphrase, summarize, estimate, discuss; in one sentence explain why aviation uses a standard temperature, describe why a log entry is required by the FAA. III Application, using abstractions in concrete situation: determine, chart, implement, prepare, solve, use, develop, explain, apply, relate, instruct, show, teaches; using a standard lapse rate, determine the temperature at a pressure altitude of 4000 feet, determine when a logbook entry is required. VI Evaluation, making judgments about the merits of ideas, materials, or phenomena: appraise, critique, judge, weigh, evaluate, select, compare and contrast, defend, interpret, support; evaluate the importance of this information for a pilot, evaluate the necessity of keeping logbook entries.

A small photo sits beside each description, with a jet in flight at the top.

From the bottom: Perception, awareness of sensory stimulus; Set, relates cues and knows; Guided Response, performs as demonstrated; Mechanism, performs simple acts well; Complex Overt Response, skillful performance of complex acts; Adaptation, modifies for special problems; Origination, new movement patterns and creativity.

scenario.title: The holding pattern that would not stick
scenario.setup: Marcus is a private pilot with 300 hours who owns a fixed-pitch four-seat airplane and wants an instrument rating for business trips. He learned to fly 20 years ago from an instructor who never had him use the flight instruments. He passed the instrument knowledge test last month after two weeks with a test-prep app. In the training device he recites the holding entry rules perfectly, but in the airplane, when ATC amends his hold to an unfamiliar fix, he freezes and stares at the course indicator. He has just come back from six weeks away, and his airplane recently got a new GPS navigator from a different maker than his old one.

questions.q: Marcus recites the entry rules but cannot use them on an amended clearance. What level of learning is he at, and what does it say about his test prep?
questions.a: Rote: he can repeat what he learned without understanding or applying it [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. Test-prep materials stress rote learning, the lowest level, which is why some applicants pass the knowledge test yet show weak knowledge in the oral [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]. Build understanding and application, and aim for correlation [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

questions.q: He freezes and stares at one instrument when the clearance changes. What is happening, and how do you shape the next lesson?
questions.a: Fixation: absorbed in one task while others slide, which is typical of beginning instrument pilots and often a sign the task has not had enough practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. He is likely in the cognitive stage, where distractions make performance fall apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Practice holds by themselves first, then add clearance changes.

questions.q: How can his 20 years of VFR flying help and hurt his instrument training?
questions.a: All new learning builds on previous experience, and prior learning can transfer positively or negatively, so you need to know his background [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Build from what he knows [[25:55|AIH 3-4]] [[25:147|AIH 7-3]], and insist on correct instrument habits from the start, because faulty habits are harder to correct later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

questions.q: What did the six-week break do to the holds he learned just before he left?
questions.a: Newly learned knowledge with little past use is recency only, and it is very vulnerable to forgetting until regular rehearsal builds frequency [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. Open with a review to activate his schemas [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].

questions.q: Why might the new GPS from a different maker cause trouble, and how do you plan for it?
questions.a: Learning one skill can hinder another (negative transfer) [[25:91|AIH 3-40]], and similar material interferes with memory most [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. Formats are not standardized, so moving to a different maker's unit should give him pause and may call for more conservative planning [[25:22|AIH 1-18]]. Teach how the system is organized, since understanding helps with variations like new avionics [[25:61|AIH 3-10]].

questions.q: Which principles of learning shape how you open the next lesson?
questions.a: Readiness: a clear objective tied to his business trips [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Effect: start with something he can succeed at [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Primacy: get the new holding technique right the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. Recency: end with a summary of the key points [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

skills.do: Explain the levels of learning aloud the way an examiner expects: name the four practical levels with their verbs, show how a learner climbs from rote to correlation on one instrument task, and say why correlation is the goal.
skills.practice: Pick one instrument task, such as holding, and write one sentence for what the learner does at each level [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Teach it to a study partner in under three minutes and have them answer with a scenario question, since the PTS asks evaluators to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].

skills.do: Describe how a physical skill is learned and taught: the psychomotor levels, the three stages of skill acquisition, telling-and-doing, knowledge of results, types of practice and plateaus, using the instrument cross-check as your example.
skills.practice: In a training device, or in the airplane with a qualified safety pilot, talk through a level-off under the hood in the three telling-and-doing steps with another applicant [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Afterward, name the stage you saw [[25:75|AIH 3-24]] and the type of practice you used [[25:77|AIH 3-26]] [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

quiz.q: A learner starts touching each switch as she reads the checklist aloud, just as she has watched you do, though you never taught it. Which learning theory explains this best?
options: Classical conditioning
Social learning
Operant conditioning
Constructivism
quiz.why: Social learning is learning by observation: watching, imitating and modeling others [[25:54|AIH 3-3]], and learners generally imitate the instructor [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with a natural one, which is not what happened here [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].

quiz.q: In operant conditioning, what association does the learner form?
options: A neutral with a natural stimulus
New with existing knowledge
An observed act with a copy of it
A behavior with its consequences
quiz.why: Operant conditioning associates a behavior with the consequences of that behavior; classical conditioning pairs a neutral environmental stimulus with a natural one [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. Relating new to existing knowledge is recoding in memory [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].

quiz.q: Which three levels of Bloom's taxonomy are the higher order thinking skills, commonly called ADM in aviation?
options: Analysis, synthesis and evaluation
Knowledge, comprehension and application
Understanding, application and correlation
Awareness, response and valuing
quiz.why: HOTS are the last three levels of Bloom's taxonomy: analysis, synthesis and evaluation, commonly called ADM [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. Knowledge, comprehension and application are the first three [[25:56|AIH 3-5]]; awareness and response are affective levels [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

quiz.q: Your learner is a high-time VFR pilot starting instrument training. Following Bruner, where do you start?
options: With abstract theory before flying
With partial panel to build respect
With the attitude flying she knows
With the hardest approach nearby
quiz.why: Bruner advocated learning from the known to the unknown and from the concrete to the abstract [[25:55|AIH 3-4]]. Read correctly, the flight instruments give essentially the same information outside references do in visual flight [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

quiz.q: Your learner sat through your partial-panel briefing and can repeat your key points word for word. What does the AIH say about this?
options: It shows she has reached correlation
It proves the briefing reached her
It does not show she can apply them
It shows the law of intensity at work
quiz.why: Learning is an active process: you cannot assume learners remember because they were present, or can apply what they know because they quote it verbatim [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]. Repeating material back is rote, the lowest level [[25:65|AIH 3-14]].

quiz.q: A learner says he is a kinesthetic learner and asks to skip the chart briefing and just fly it. What is the AIH-based answer?
options: Most use all styles; you will mix them
Agree, and teach him only hands-on from now on
Tell him learning styles were disproven
Move him to a lecture-only course
quiz.why: Learners generally use all three VAK styles, with one dominant that can change with the task [[25:73|AIH 3-22]], and a variety of styles should be addressed in every lesson [[25:74|AIH 3-23]]. The AIH notes controversy about learning styles but does not say they are disproven [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

quiz.q: In early hood lessons your learner stares at the attitude indicator and ignores the rest. Which principle is the main reason to fix it now rather than later?
options: Recency
Intensity
Readiness
Primacy
quiz.why: What is learned first creates a strong, almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]], and in initial instrument training, emphasis on a single instrument can become a habit if not corrected [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

quiz.q: On an instrument proficiency check, ATC assigns an unexpected hold just after your pilot admits holds make her nervous. You brief holding right then. Which principle are you using?
options: Primacy, by teaching it right first
Readiness, through a teachable moment
Exercise, through more repetitions
Recency, through the final summary
quiz.why: Readiness includes the teachable moment, when a person is especially responsive to being taught; the AIH says these can be found or created even in an instrument proficiency check [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

quiz.q: Your learner flies RNAV approaches to standard in the practice area but loses the plot when ATC amends her clearance on a real trip. Which level has she reached, and what is the goal?
options: Application; correlation is the goal
Rote; understanding is the goal
Correlation; application is the goal
Understanding; rote is the goal
quiz.why: Practicing to consistency after a demonstration is the application level, where instructors too often stop. Correlation, tying the element to other blocks of learning, should be the objective [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

quiz.q: Which key verbs does the AIH give for the understanding level?
options: Define, identify, label
Determine, develop, solve
Describe, estimate, explain
Create, design, plan
quiz.why: Understanding uses describe, estimate or explain; rote uses define, identify and label; application uses determine, develop and solve [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. Create, design and plan are synthesis verbs [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

quiz.q: Under the hood your learner holds altitude well until you ask for a frequency change; then the heading wanders. Which stage of skill acquisition is this?
options: Associative
Cognitive
Automatic response
Habit
quiz.why: In the cognitive stage the skill takes all the learner's attention, and distractions cause performance to deteriorate or stop [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Habit is a psychomotor level, not a stage [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].

quiz.q: When does the AIH say a learner reaches the habit level of the psychomotor domain?
options: After three or four repetitions
When she can explain every step to you
When she flies it with no errors at all
Doing it within twice the expert's time
quiz.why: The habit level is reached when the learner can perform the skill in twice the time it takes the instructor or an expert [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]. Three or four repetitions is a retention finding about meaningful repetition [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

quiz.q: About how long, and how much, does short-term memory hold?
options: About 5 minutes and three chunks
About 30 seconds and seven chunks
About 10 seconds and twelve chunks
A lifetime, with no limit at all
quiz.why: STM stores information roughly 30 seconds and holds about seven bits or chunks [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Relatively permanent, unlimited storage describes long-term memory [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].

quiz.q: A pilot moves from one manufacturer's GPS navigator to another and keeps pressing buttons in the old order. What is this, and what does the AIH advise?
options: Negative transfer; plan more conservatively
Positive transfer; no change is needed
Fading; review the old unit's manual
Generativity; let him explore freely
quiz.why: When learning skill A hinders skill B, negative transfer occurs [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Formats are not standardized, so moving between manufacturers should give the pilot pause and may call for more conservative planning [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot rolls into turns with rudder and never notices doing it. Which theory explains how the brain frees attention this way?
options: Classical conditioning
Social learning theory
Information processing theory
Constructivism
final_quiz.why: Information processing theory says the brain lets habitual, routine things go unnoticed, like pressing the rudder in a turn, leaving conscious thought free for other issues [[25:56|AIH 3-5]].

final_quiz.q: You revisit attitude instrument flying on every lesson, each time at a higher level, from straight-and-level to partial-panel approaches. Which concept is that?
options: Bruner's spiral curriculum
Dewey's reflective thought
Piaget's assimilation
Sensory precoding
final_quiz.why: The spiral curriculum revisits basic ideas repeatedly and builds on them in more sophisticated ways [[25:55|AIH 3-4]]; Bill does the same with aerodynamics, a constant thread in his flight lessons [[25:56|AIH 3-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner says, 'I check the weather before departure, get updates every hour and divert at the first suspicion of weather ahead.' What does the AIH call this?
options: A problem-solving tactic
A learning plateau
An affective level
A cognitive strategy
final_quiz.why: Cognitive strategies are knowledge of how to do something, and this strategy for avoiding inadvertent IMC at night is the AIH example [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]. Problem-solving tactics are narrower, specific actions for a particular result, like using a ruler on a takeoff chart [[25:83|AIH 3-32]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner picks up your habit of skipping the briefing on familiar approaches, though it was never in your lesson plan. Which characteristic does the AIH tie to this kind of incidental learning?
options: Learning is purposeful
Learning is multifaceted
Learning is an active process
Learning is a result of experience
final_quiz.why: Learning is multifaceted: while learning the subject at hand, learners may also develop attitudes about aviation, good or bad. The AIH calls this incidental learning [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

final_quiz.q: An owner-pilot only seems interested in the parts of the course that help him reach his customers' airports in IFR. What does the AIH say to do?
options: Tell him goals do not change the syllabus
Use threats of failure until he is serious
Skip every topic he says he does not need
Relate each new lesson to his goals
final_quiz.why: Learning is purposeful: learners learn from activities that further their goals, and instructors need to relate new learning to the learner's goals [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]. Threats do not promote effective learning [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

final_quiz.q: First lesson with a new instrument learner. Which plan best fits the law of effect?
options: Tasks she can master, then praise first
Partial-panel unusual attitudes to humble her
A warning that she will fail without more work
Six approaches in a row and no debrief at all
final_quiz.why: Behaviors with satisfying outcomes tend to be repeated, so create situations that promote success [[25:63|AIH 3-12]], and comment on progress before areas to improve [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. The AIH's example of a weakened connection is teaching landings on the first flight [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

final_quiz.q: Which instructor habit applies the principle of recency?
options: Teaching each procedure right the first time
Dramatic, realistic scenarios in the simulator
A planned summary of key points at the end
Checking that basic needs are met before flight
final_quiz.why: Instructors apply recency when they plan a summary and repeat important points at the end of a lesson or critique [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. The other choices describe primacy, intensity and readiness [[25:62|AIH 3-11]] [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

final_quiz.q: Using Figure 3-9, which level is the objective 'Design a personal minimums checklist for IFR departures'?
options: Knowledge
Synthesis
Comprehension
Application
final_quiz.why: Synthesis puts parts together into a new and integrated whole, with verbs such as create, design and plan [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Knowledge, comprehension and application are the first three levels [[25:56|AIH 3-5]].

final_quiz.q: A learner passed the instrument knowledge test using only a test-prep app, but in the oral she cannot explain how an approach is built. What does the AIH say explains this?
options: She reached correlation but forgot it
The oral tests the affective domain
She has an auditory learning style
The app stressed rote, the lowest level
final_quiz.why: Test preparation materials emphasize rote learning, the lowest of all levels, and examiners report applicants who pass the knowledge test easily yet lack knowledge in oral questioning [[25:131|AIH 5-28]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner levels off late from descents again and again. You plan to save it all for the postflight debrief. What does the AIH say?
options: Tell her soon; do not let her practice it
Saving it is best; feedback in flight distracts
Ignore it; she will discover it on her own
Wait for the stage check and grade it then
final_quiz.why: Learners should be told about errors as soon after the performance as possible and should not be allowed to practice mistakes, since unlearning a mistake is harder than learning correctly the first time [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the telling-and-doing technique have the learner talk you through a maneuver while you fly it?
options: To give the instructor a break from talking
To grade her for the practical test record
To check understanding before she flies
To replace her own practice of the maneuver
final_quiz.why: In learner tells, instructor does, the learner organizes her thoughts free of flying, and the instructor can evaluate understanding and correct it before she is absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

final_quiz.q: Studies of deliberate practice suggest which condition gives the best results while a learner works on holding entries?
options: Constant ATC calls mixed into each entry
Few distractions, brief explicit feedback
A long explanation before every attempt
Only a grade, with no feedback between
final_quiz.why: During deliberate practice, learners do better if distractions are avoided, and feedback should be brief and explicit [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. A long, detailed explanation before performing is confusing [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: After quick early gains, your learner's approach scores have been flat for three lessons. Which response fits the AIH?
options: Call it normal; work another area awhile
Add more of the same approach until it breaks
Warn her she may not be suited to IFR flying
Stop all feedback so she feels less pressure
final_quiz.why: A plateau is normal and temporary: prepare the learner for it and move to a different place in the curriculum. Over-practice can bring one on [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

final_quiz.q: A CFII taught a certain approach type often years ago but not since, and now cannot recall its details quickly. Which usage pattern is this?
options: Recency only
Frequency and recency
Precoding
Frequency only
final_quiz.why: Knowledge used much in the past but not recently is frequency only: retrieved slowly or not at all until recent practice refreshes it [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. An instructor's knowledge is just as vulnerable to forgetting [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].

final_quiz.q: Which study plan gives the best memory results, according to the AIH?
options: One long cram the night before
Short sessions spaced regularly
Rereading with no study questions
Listening to a lecture passively
final_quiz.why: Shorter, regularly spaced study sessions give memory results that far exceed cramming, and writing study questions helps [[25:92|AIH 3-41]]. Passive lecture listeners keep roughly five percent over 24 hours [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

final_quiz.q: To help your instrument learner transfer holding skills to unfamiliar fixes, which approach does the AIH support?
options: The same hold at the home fix only
Entries by rote, and stop there
Varied practice, little needless rote
Show new uses at the checkride
final_quiz.why: Practicing under a variety of conditions gives positive transfer [[25:90|AIH 3-39]], and unnecessary rote learning should be avoided since it does not foster transfer [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner trained VFR with integrated flight instruction from the first lesson. What does that give him now, and what should he have been told?
options: Full IMC skill, so less training is needed
Nothing, since VFR and IFR skills differ
Negative transfer that must be unlearned
A habit foundation, not IMC readiness
final_quiz.why: Integrated instruction builds habits of cross-check, interpretation and control that give a firm foundation for an instrument rating [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], but learners must understand it does not prepare them for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

takeaways: The PTS's seven items map to AIH Chapter 3; the principles of learning are the six laws.
No single learning theory fits every learner: reinforce, model and build understanding together.
Learning is purposeful, experience-based, multifaceted and active, so make the learner do and decide.
Teach every lesson toward correlation, and write objectives at a level with the AIH verbs.
Physical skills grow from cognitive to associative to automatic: demonstrate, let the learner tell, then do, and give fast feedback.
Mix your practice, expect plateaus, and watch for overlearning that drops the thinking.
Memory runs sensory to short-term to long-term; frequency and recency of use decide what comes back.
Plan for transfer: vary the conditions, avoid needless rote, and build correct habits from the first lesson.
cfi_notes: The PTS lists these items for the older FAA-H-8083-9 [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS I.A]]. In the 9B, the principles of learning are the laws of learning [[25:62|AIH 3-11]], and learning physical skills is spread over the psychomotor domain [[25:68|AIH 3-17]], Acquiring Skill Knowledge [[25:74|AIH 3-23]] and the telling-and-doing technique [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Use the 9B terms, but recognize the PTS words when an examiner uses them.

Two lists sound alike: the six principles (laws) of learning [[25:62|AIH 3-11]] and the five principles of retention (praise, association, favorable attitudes, all senses, meaningful repetition) [[25:89|AIH 3-38]] [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]. Say which list you mean.

The AIH is not consistent on where the HOTS sit. Chapter 3 gives the four practical levels and then calls analysis, synthesis and evaluation the three higher levels [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[25:66|AIH 3-15]], while Chapter 6 equates analyzing, synthesizing and evaluating with the application and correlation levels [[25:139|AIH 6-8]]. Teach the Chapter 3 picture and know the Chapter 6 wording in case an examiner quotes it.
The AIH names the third stage of skill acquisition both 'automaticity' and 'automatic response' on the same page [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Either name is correct.
Psychomotor levels: the text gives four practical levels for aviation, while Figure 3-12 shows seven [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]. Teach the four, and know the seven exist if the figure comes up.

Per the PTS NOTE for Area I, the evaluator selects at least Tasks E, F and G and one other, so this Task may or may not be tested on a given flight instructor checkride [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS Area I NOTE]]. The PTS also tells evaluators to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions where possible [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], so prepare one instrument example for each of the seven items.

The AIH says some research indicates three or four repetitions give the maximum effect, in its section on meaningful repetition and retention [[25:90|AIH 3-39]], while its skill sections say progress depends on repeated practice and that over-practice can bring on a plateau [[25:76|AIH 3-25]] [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. It does not reconcile the two, so do not quote 'three or four' as a limit on approaches flown.

Learning styles: the AIH notes controversy over their scientific value [[25:71|AIH 3-20]] but still tells instructors to address a variety in every lesson [[25:74|AIH 3-23]]. In an oral, give both halves.
gaps: The AIH gives no aviation example of classical conditioning; it uses only Pavlov's dog [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].

No source says how many repetitions of an instrument maneuver or approach one lesson should hold. The AIH says beginners reach a point where more practice is harmful [[25:78|AIH 3-27]] and that some research indicates three or four repetitions give the maximum effect for retention [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]; the rest is instructor judgment.
The habit-level rule needs an expert's time [[25:68|AIH 3-17]], but no source gives standard times for instrument tasks. Time yourself or another experienced pilot.

No source says how fast instrument skills fade without practice. The AIH says even automatic skills may not stay automatic after disuse [[25:92|AIH 3-41]], and AC 61-98E says instrument-rated pilots who are not proficient are susceptible to loss of control in IMC [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.5]].
The PTS references FAA-H-8083-9; this lesson uses only the current 9B, so any older-edition terms the 9B dropped are not covered here.
The AIH points to a free learning-style questionnaire on a website [[25:72|AIH 3-21]], but no source here validates any learning-style test.

activities.title: True or false: building a skill
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Blocked practice can fool both the learner and the instructor into thinking a skill is well learned.
cards.why: True. Blocked practice gives better short-term performance but poorer long-term learning, and it fools both [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

cards.s: A beginning learner always benefits from a longer practice period.
cards.why: False. A beginner reaches a point where more practice is unproductive or even harmful; experienced learners profit from longer periods [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

cards.s: A learning plateau means learning has stopped.
cards.why: False. A plateau does not necessarily mean learning has ceased, and in motor skills it is normal [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

cards.s: An instructor can bring on a learning plateau by over-practice.
Skill practice benefits when the instructor introduces new ideas during it.
cards.why: False. Unlike acquiring knowledge, skill learning does not benefit from new ideas introduced during practice [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

cards.s: In the automatic response stage, a learner may no longer be able to explain the steps.
cards.why: True. The learner may say, 'I have developed a feel for it' [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

activities.title: An instrument course, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFII for Priya, a private pilot with 160 hours who is starting her instrument rating in a fixed-pitch trainer. Make each call as her training unfolds.

steps.s: First hood lesson. She asks you to skip the talk-through because she is 'a visual learner'.
options: Agree, and teach her only with pictures and charts from now on
Explain that people use several styles, and keep a mix in every lesson
Tell her learning styles are a myth and lecture as planned
Skip the hood work and give her a video to watch at home instead
steps.why: Learners generally use all three styles, with one dominant that can change with the task [[25:73|AIH 3-22]], and every lesson should address a variety of styles [[25:74|AIH 3-23]].

steps.s: Under the hood she stares at the attitude indicator while the heading drifts, and an ATC call makes it worse.
options: Add more radio calls right away so she learns to cope with them
Take the controls and fly the rest of the lesson yourself
Give her more practice of the scan alone, then add other tasks
Move her on to steep turns to raise the challenge level
steps.why: Fixation is often a sign the task has not had enough practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]], and in the cognitive stage distractions make performance fall apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Single-instrument emphasis can become a habit if not corrected [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

steps.s: Three lessons of the same ILS: her scores rose fast, then went flat.
options: Explain plateaus are normal and work on holds for a while
Fly the same ILS six more times to push through the plateau
Tell her she may not be cut out for instrument flying
Stop giving feedback so she can relax and enjoy the flying
steps.why: A plateau is normal and temporary; move to a different place in the curriculum, and remember over-practice can cause it [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. The same drill again is blocked practice [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

steps.s: She flies holds well in the training device but misjudges an entry at an unfamiliar fix in the airplane.
options: Drill the same device hold again until it is perfect
Teach the entry rules by rote and test her recall of them
Move on, since she already met the standard in the device
Vary the fixes, winds and clearances so the skill transfers
steps.why: Practicing under a variety of conditions gives positive transfer [[25:90|AIH 3-39]], and unnecessary rote learning does not foster transfer [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

steps.s: Back on the ground for the debrief.
options: Give a grade only, since a number tells her where she stands
Ask for her self-assessment, compare it with yours, and lead with progress
List every error in the order it happened, then add the good parts
Skip it, since the flight went well and she is tired
steps.why: Collaborative assessment starts with the learner's self-assessment, followed by a discussion comparing it with the instructor's [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Positive comments on progress come before areas to improve [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].
